candidate.educational_objective: Recognize excessive vancomycin AUC exposure with worsening renal function and escalate for AUC-guided dosing reassessment.

options.A: Continue the same regimen because serious MRSA infection generally requires higher vancomycin exposure even when the serum creatinine begins to rise.
options.B: Notify the provider or pharmacist and anticipate reassessment of vancomycin dosing and renal function because the AUC exceeds the recommended exposure range.
options.C: Increase the next dose while extending the interval, because preserving a large individual dose is more important than reducing total exposure during kidney injury.
options.D: Ignore the AUC result and use trough-only dosing because a single pre-dose concentration remains the preferred safety target despite rising creatinine.

candidate.rationale: For serious MRSA infection, the current ASHP/PIDS/SIDP/IDSA vancomycin monitoring guideline recommends AUC-guided dosing with a target AUC/MIC of 400–600 mg·h/L when MIC is assumed to be 1 mg/L. An AUC of 690 together with a substantial creatinine rise raises concern for excessive exposure and nephrotoxicity and warrants prompt dosing and renal-function reassessment. Trough-only targeting of 15–20 mg/L is no longer the preferred safety strategy because it has been associated with greater nephrotoxicity.

candidate.stem: A client receiving IV vancomycin for a serious MRSA infection has an estimated 24-hour AUC of 690 mg·h/L and serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
